sec:appendix_small_seq.section: Dealing with Sequences Shorter than the Read Length

nodes.name: Number of species $N$
nodes.statement: We denote by $N$ the number of species in the database.

nodes.name: Species sequences $S_1,..,S_N$ and alphabet $\Upsilon$
nodes.statement: The species' 16S rRNA sequences are marked $S_1,..,S_N$, represented as strings over the alphabet $\Upsilon = \{\text{`A', `C', `G', `T'}\}$.

nodes.name: Distinct database sequences
nodes.statement: We assume that the $S_i$'s are {\it distinct} sequences.

nodes.name: Sequence lengths $n_i$
nodes.statement: The sequences may have {\it different} lengths $n_1,..,n_N$, with $n_i$ the length of the i-th species' sequence, i.e. $S_i \in \Upsilon^{n_i}$.

nodes.name: Maximum sequence length $n_{MAX}$
nodes.statement: We define the maximum sequence length as $n_{MAX} \equiv \max_{i} n_i$.

nodes.name: Nucleotide and substring notation $s_{i,j}$, $s_{i,j:k}$
nodes.statement: We denote by $s_{i,j}$ the j-th nucleotide in the i-th species' sequence $S_i$, and by $s_{i,j:k}$ the substring containing nucleotides $j, j+1, .., k$ in the sequence $S_i$.

nodes.name: Species frequency vector ${\mathbf x}$
nodes.statement: We represent the proportion of each species in the mixture using a vector ${\mathbf x}$ of length $N$, with $x_i$ the frequency of species $i$.

nodes.name: Probability simplex $\Delta_N$
nodes.statement: We have ${\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$, where $\Delta_N$ is the $N$-dimensional simplex, $\Delta_N = \{ {\mathbf x} \: : \: x_i \geq 0, \: \sum_{i=1}^N x_i = 1 \}$.

nodes.name: Interior of a set $int(\mathcal{A})$
nodes.statement: We represent the interior of a set $\mathcal{A}$ as $int(\mathcal{A})$.

nodes.name: Interior of the simplex $int(\Delta_N)$
nodes.statement: In particular, $int(\Delta_N)$ is the subset of $\Delta_N$ containing vectors with positive entries, $int(\Delta_N) = \{ {\mathbf x} \: : \: x_i > 0, \: \sum_{i=1}^N x_i = 1 \}$.

nodes.name: Reads $r_1,..,r_R$ of length $L$
nodes.statement: We observe data in the form of $R$ reads of length $L$, $r_1, .., r_R \in \Upsilon^L$, with \ensuremath{L}\: typically around $\sim\!50\!-\!400$, as in the Illumina and 454 sequencing technologies.

nodes.name: Read frequency vector ${\mathbf y}$
nodes.statement: We represent the data by a vector of read frequencies, ${\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^L}$, with the {\it j}-th coordinate given by $y_j = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{i=1}^R 1_{\{lex(r_i) = j\}}, \quad \forall j=1,..,4^L$.
nodes.statement_short: ${\mathbf y}\in\Delta_{4^L}$ is the empirical frequency of each of the $4^L$ possible reads.

nodes.name: Lexicographic read index $lex(r)$
nodes.statement: Here $lex(r)$ is the index of $r$ in the lexicographic ordering of all $4^L$ possible reads (i.e. $lex(\text{'AAA ... A'}) = 1, .., lex(\text{'TTT ... T'}) = 4^L$).

nodes.name: Inverse lexicographic transformation $lex^{-1}$
nodes.statement: We also define the inverse lexicographic ordering transformation, $lex^{-1}$, which for a given index $j$ gives the corresponding sequence (e.g. $lex^{-1}(18) = \text{'AAA ... ATC'}$).

nodes.name: Microbial Community Reconstruction (MCR) problem
nodes.statement: In the {\textbf {MCR} } problem, the data vector ${\mathbf y}$ and the database sequences $S_1,..,S_N$ are given as input. Our goal is to reconstruct the species frequencies vector ${\mathbf x}$ from this information.
nodes.statement_short: Given read frequencies ${\mathbf y}$ and database sequences $S_1..S_N$, reconstruct species frequencies ${\mathbf x}$.

nodes.name: Number of unique reads $M$
nodes.statement: The vector ${\mathbf y}$ is of exponential length $(4^L)$ but very sparse, with only $M \leq R$ non-zero coordinates, where $M$ is the number of {\it unique} sequence reads.

nodes.name: Two-step read sampling model and read-sampling matrix $A$
nodes.statement: We assume that the $R$ reads are sampled identically and independently (i.i.d.) from the set of amplified regions in two steps, \begin{enumerate} \item First, sample a microbial species $b$ from the set of possible species $\{1,..,N\}$, with the probability of species $j$ being sampled proportional to the amount of DNA from this species, $x'_j \equiv Pr(b = j) = \frac{x_j n_j}{\sum_{i=1}^N x_i n_i}$. \item Next, sample a read $r$ from a distribution given by the species $b$. We represent sampling probabilities using a $4^L \times N$ read-sampling matrix $A = A(S, L)$ whose $(i,j)$-th entry is the probability to observe read $i$ given that we know it came from species $j$, $A_{ij} = Pr(r = i | b = j)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Reads are i.i.d.: pick species $b$ with probability $\propto x_j n_j$, then a read $i$ with probability $A_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Length re-weighting $x'$ vs $x$ disregarded
nodes.statement: The vector of sampling probabilities ${\mathbf x}'$ from step 1 is obtained by re-weighting the frequency vector ${\mathbf x}$ according to the sequence lengths. For ease of notation, we disregard this re-weighting, and denote both vectors as ${\mathbf x}$. When all sequences lengths $n_j$ are identical we have indeed ${\mathbf x}'={\mathbf x}$. More generally, the vectors are different but we can easily convert ${\mathbf x}$ to ${\mathbf x}'$ or ${\mathbf x}'$ to ${\mathbf x}$ using the above relation $x'_j = \frac{x_j n_j}{\sum_{i=1}^N x_i n_i}$
nodes.statement_short: The length-weighted sampling vector ${\mathbf x}'$ is identified with ${\mathbf x}$; they coincide for equal lengths and convert easily.

nodes.name: Read distribution $P_{\mathbf x}({\mathbf y};A,L)$
nodes.statement: The sampling process defines a probability distribution $P_{{\mathbf x}} = P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf y} ; A, L)$ on the space of possible frequencies $\Delta_{4^L}$, \begin{align} P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf y} ; A, L) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \sum_{j=1}^N A_{ij} x_j \:\:\quad & \quad\:\: {\mathbf y} = {\mathbf e}^{(i)} \\ 0 \:\:\quad & \quad\:\: \mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \end{align} \vspace{-0.15cm} \noindent where ${\mathbf e}^{(i)} \in \Delta_{4^L}$ is the i-th vector in the standard basis, $e^{(i)}_i =1, e^{(i)}_j =0 \: \forall j \neq i$.
nodes.statement_short: One read is distributed on the basis vectors ${\mathbf e}^{(i)}$ of $\Delta_{4^L}$ with probability $[A{\mathbf x}]_i$.

nodes.name: Mixture model for a single read
nodes.statement: P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf y} ; A, L) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \sum_{j=1}^N A_{ij} x_j \:\:\quad & \quad\:\: {\mathbf y} = {\mathbf e}^{(i)} \\ 0 \:\:\quad & \quad\:\: \mbox{otherwise} \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:mixture_model

nodes.name: Reads as i.i.d. random vectors ${\mathbf y}^{(i)}$
nodes.statement: The data can be represented as $R$ i.i.d. random variables, ${\mathbf y}^{(1)}, .., {\mathbf y}^{(R)} \sim P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf y} ; A, L)$, with the sample frequency ${\mathbf y}$ represented as, ${\mathbf y} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{i=1}^R {\mathbf y}^{(i)}$.

nodes.name: Problem ${\textbf {MCR}}(L,A)$
nodes.statement: We denote the {\textbf {MCR} } problem with read sampling matrix $A$ by ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$.

nodes.name: Uniform error-free read-sampling matrix
nodes.statement: In its simplest form, $A$ can be constructed as follows, \begin{equation} A_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n_j-L+1} 1_{\{lex^{-1}(i) = s_{j,k:k+L-1}\}}}{n_j-L+1} \end{equation} This matrix represents {\it uniform} sampling of {\it error-free} reads along the sequence of the chosen species $j$, assuming $L \leq n_j \: \forall j$.
nodes.statement_short: $A_{ij}$ is the fraction of the $n_j-L+1$ length-$L$ windows of $S_j$ equal to read $i$.

nodes.name: Uniform tail for reads longer than the sequence
nodes.statement: If $L > n_i$ we assume that the `tail' of each read is sampled uniformly from $\Upsilon$ (see Appendix Section \ref{sec:appendix_small_seq}).

nodes.name: Extending $A$ to errors and biases; model limitations
nodes.statement: The above construction of $A$ assumes no read errors and no biases. Incorporating more realistic sequencing models with non-uniform read density due to amplification biases, read errors (substitutions and indels), alignments errors etc. can be done by changing the definition of $A$ from eq. (\ref{eq:MixMatrix}). The same database $S$ may thus yield different matrices $A$, and the statistical and algorithmic properties of a certain {\textbf {MCR} } problem depend on the database $S$ only through the matrix $A$. The assumption in step $1$ is that species DNA fragments are sampled according to their DNA frequencies out of the total DNA present in a sample. The model cannot accommodate deviations from this assumption which may arise from amplification biases and limited library complexity, which may distort the species frequencies - that is, the fraction of reads originating from a certain species may not represent the species' true frequency in the mixture. Accounting and correcting for such biases require analyzing multiple samples together.
nodes.statement_short: Errors and biases are modeled by changing $A$; the problem depends on the database only through $A$; amplification biases are not modeled.

nodes.name: Estimator $\hat{{\mathbf x}}$
nodes.statement: An estimator $\hat{{\mathbf x}}$ of the frequency vector ${\mathbf x}$ is simply a function from the set of all reads and database, to the $n$-dimensional simplex, $\hat{{\mathbf x}}: \Delta_{4^L} \times \mathcal{S} \to \Delta_N, \: \hat{{\mathbf x}} = \hat{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf y}, S)$ (here $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of all possible sequences databases, i.e. the space of all ordered finite collections of strings over $\Upsilon$).
nodes.genus: a function from the set of all reads and database, to the $n$-dimensional simplex

nodes.name: Empirical loss minimization over the simplex
nodes.statement: We can solve the {\textbf {MCR} } problem by finding an estimator $\hat{{\mathbf x}}$ minimizing an empirical loss function. That is, define $\hat{{\mathbf y}} = A \hat{{\mathbf x}}$, the empirical reads distribution given the estimator $\hat{{\mathbf x}}$. We would like to minimize the loss $l(\hat{{\mathbf y}}, y)$, and define the following estimator, \begin{equation} \hat{{\mathbf x}} = argmin_{{\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N} l(A {\mathbf x}, {\mathbf y}) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Estimate ${\mathbf x}$ by minimizing a loss $l(A{\mathbf x},{\mathbf y})$ over the simplex $\Delta_N$.

nodes.name: Loss-minimizing estimator over the simplex
nodes.statement: \hat{{\mathbf x}} = argmin_{{\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N} l(A {\mathbf x}, {\mathbf y})
nodes.label: eq:optproblem

nodes.name: Kullback-Leibler loss $l_{KL}$
nodes.statement: A natural loss function is the Kullback-Leibler divergence $l_{KL}({\mathbf y}, \hat{{\mathbf y}}) = D(P_{{\mathbf y}} || P_{\hat{{\mathbf y}}})$.

nodes.name: KL loss minimization is maximum likelihood
nodes.statement: This formulation is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the data ${\mathbf y}$, according to the probabilistic model in eq. (\ref{eq:mixture_model}).
conclusions: This formulation is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the data ${\mathbf y}$

nodes.name: $l_2$ loss
nodes.statement: We choose instead the $l_2$ loss $l_{2}({\mathbf y}, \hat{{\mathbf y}}) = ||{\mathbf y} - \hat{{\mathbf y}}||_2$, mainly for computational considerations.

nodes.name: $l_1$ relaxation is vacuous on the simplex
nodes.statement: The most common remedy of replacing the $l_0$ norm by the convex $l_1$ norm does not work in our problem since for probability vectors in the simplex ${\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$ the constraint $||{\mathbf x}||_1=1$ trivially holds.

nodes.name: Euclidean reconstruction error $\mathcal{D}_{l_2}$
nodes.statement: We use the simple $l_2$ norm as a representative of this group. This metric measures the deviation in species {\it frequencies} between the true and reconstructed solutions, $\mathcal{D}_{l_2}({\mathbf x}, \hat{{\mathbf x}}) = \sqrt{ \sum_{i=1}^M (x_i - \hat{x}_i)^2}$.

nodes.name: Phylogenetically-aware Mahalanobis distance $\mathcal{D}_{MA}$
nodes.statement: We propose a novel Phylogenetically-aware criterion, using a Mahalanobis distance, \\ $\mathcal{D}_{MA}({\mathbf x}, \hat{{\mathbf x}}; D) = \sqrt{ ({\mathbf x} - \hat{{\mathbf x}})^{\top} D ({\mathbf x} - \hat{{\mathbf x}}) } = \sqrt{ \sum_{i,j} D_{ij} (x_i - \hat{x}_i) (x_j - \hat{x}_j) }$. The matrix $D$ is constructed to capture the phylogenetic distance between species (for example, from the species 16S rRNA sequences themselves). High (low) values of $D_{ij}$ correspond to pairs of species $(i,j)$ which are closely-related (remote).
differentia: The matrix $D$ is constructed to capture the phylogenetic distance between species
nodes.statement_short: Error metric $\sqrt{({\mathbf x}-\hat{{\mathbf x}})^\top D({\mathbf x}-\hat{{\mathbf x}})}$ with $D$ a species-similarity matrix.

nodes.name: Weight matrix $D = A^{\top} A$
nodes.statement: For concreteness, we choose specifically $D = A^{\top} A$, which represent the similarity between species based on their 16S rRNA sequences.

nodes.name: Identifiability of ${\textbf {MCR}}(L,A)$
nodes.statement: We say that the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is identifiable, if for every ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \neq {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$, there exists ${\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^L}$ such that $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(1)}}({\mathbf y}; A; L) \neq P_{{\mathbf x}^{(2)}}({\mathbf y}; A; L)$.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct frequency vectors always give distinct read distributions.
nodes.label: def:identifiability

nodes.name: Rank criterion for identifiability
nodes.statement: Let $A_{(1)}$ be the matrix constructed from $A$, concatenated with an all $1$'s row vector ${\textbf 1_N}$, $ A_{(1)} \equiv \left( \begin{array}{c} A \\ {\textbf 1_N} \\ \end{array} \right) $. The reconstruction problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is identifiable if and only if $rank(A_{(1)}) = N$.
assumptions: Let $A_{(1)}$ be the matrix constructed from $A$, concatenated with an all $1$'s row vector ${\textbf 1_N}$
conclusions: The reconstruction problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is identifiable if and only if $rank(A_{(1)}) = N$.
nodes.statement_short: MCR(L,A) is identifiable iff $A$ stacked with an all-ones row has full column rank $N$.
nodes.label: prop:identifiability

nodes.name: Critical read length for identifiability
nodes.statement: Assume $N > 4$. Suppose that the database $S$ is composed of $N$ distinct sequences such that no sequence is a substring of another sequence, i.e. $s_{i,j:k} \neq s_{i'} \: \forall i \neq i' \in \{1,..,N\}, \forall j,k \in \{1,..,n_i\}$. Let $A^{(u,L)}$ be the sampling matrix obtained by {\it uniform} sampling of reads with read length $L$, according to eq. (\ref{eq:MixMatrix}). Then there is a critical read length $L_c$, $1 < L_c \leq \max_i n_i$ such that the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A^{(u,L)})$ is identifiable if and only if $L \geq L_c$.
assumptions: the database $S$ is composed of $N$ distinct sequences such that no sequence is a substring of another sequence
Let $A^{(u,L)}$ be the sampling matrix obtained by {\it uniform} sampling of reads with read length $L$, according to eq. (\ref{eq:MixMatrix}).
conclusions: there is a critical read length $L_c$, $1 < L_c \leq \max_i n_i$ such that the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A^{(u,L)})$ is identifiable if and only if $L \geq L_c$.
nodes.statement_short: For substring-free databases with $N>4$, uniform-read MCR is identifiable exactly for read lengths above a threshold $L_c\in(1,n_{MAX}]$.
nodes.label: prop:identifiability_vs_L

nodes.name: Relaxing the substring-free and uniform-sampling assumptions
nodes.statement: We assume that no sequence in the database is a substring of another database sequence for mathematical convenience. This assumption usually holds in practice provided a long enough region is sequenced, and can be relaxed while still obtaining similar identifiability results. In addition, we demonstrated identifiability for a uniform read sampling distribution, but a similar result can be obtained for other read sampling distributions.
nodes.statement_short: The substring-free assumption is for convenience and the result extends to non-uniform read sampling.

nodes.name: Partial identifiability for species $j$
nodes.statement: We say that the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$, if for any ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$ such that $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(1)}} ({\mathbf y} ; A, L) = P_{{\mathbf x}^{(2)}} ({\mathbf y} ; A, L) \: \forall {\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^L}$, we have $x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Any two frequency vectors with the same read distribution agree on the frequency of species $j$.
nodes.label: def:partial_identifiability

nodes.name: Null-space criterion for partial identifiability
nodes.statement: The problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$, if and only if the standard basis vector ${\mathbf e}^{(j)} \in \Delta_N$ is orthogonal to the null-space of $A_{(1)}$, that is $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow x_j=0 \: \forall {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$.
conclusions: The problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$, if and only if the standard basis vector ${\mathbf e}^{(j)} \in \Delta_N$ is orthogonal to the null-space of $A_{(1)}$, that is $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow x_j=0 \: \forall {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$.
equivalent_conditions: The problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$
the standard basis vector ${\mathbf e}^{(j)} \in \Delta_N$ is orthogonal to the null-space of $A_{(1)}$
nodes.statement_short: Species $j$ is identifiable iff every null vector of $A_{(1)}$ has zero $j$-th coordinate.
nodes.label: prop:partial_identifiability

nodes.name: Finite-sample reconstruction error bounds ($l_2$ and Mahalanobis)
nodes.statement: Consider the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ with $R$ sequence reads, and let $\hat{{\mathbf x}}$ be the estimator minimizing the $l_2$ loss, $\hat{{\mathbf x}} = argmin_{{\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N} l_2(A {\mathbf x}, {\mathbf y})$. Then, \begin{enumerate} \item Let $\lambda_{\min}(A^{\top}A)$ be the smallest eigenvalue of $A^{\top}A$. The Euclidian $l_2$ distance satisfies: \vspace{-0.1cm} \begin{equation} Pr\Big(\mathcal{D}_{l_2}(\hat{{\mathbf x}}, {{\mathbf x}}^*) \leq \frac{2 + \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{R\lambda_{\min}(A^{\top}A)} }\Big) \geq 1-\delta, \quad \forall \delta \in (0,1). \end{equation} \vspace{-0.1cm} \item The Mahalanobis distance with weight matrix $A^{\top} A$ satisfies: \vspace{-0.1cm} \begin{equation} Pr \Big( \mathcal{D}_{MA}(\hat{{\mathbf x}}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{\top} A) \leq \frac{2 + \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{R}}\Big) \geq 1-\delta, \quad \forall \delta \in (0,1). \end{equation} \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Consider the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ with $R$ sequence reads

Let $\lambda_{\min}(A^{\top}A)$ be the smallest eigenvalue of $A^{\top}A$.
conclusions: The Mahalanobis distance with weight matrix $A^{\top} A$ satisfies:

nodes.statement_short: With prob. $1-\delta$ the $l_2$ estimator has Mahalanobis error $\le(2+\sqrt{\log 1/\delta})/\sqrt R$, and $l_2$ error that over $\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(A^\top A)}$.
nodes.label: prop:reconstruction_error_bound

nodes.name: $l_2$ error bound
nodes.statement: Pr\Big(\mathcal{D}_{l_2}(\hat{{\mathbf x}}, {{\mathbf x}}^*) \leq \frac{2 + \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{R\lambda_{\min}(A^{\top}A)} }\Big) \geq 1-\delta, \quad \forall \delta \in (0,1).
nodes.label: eq:l2_bound

nodes.name: Mahalanobis error bound
nodes.statement: Pr \Big( \mathcal{D}_{MA}(\hat{{\mathbf x}}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{\top} A) \leq \frac{2 + \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{R}}\Big) \geq 1-\delta, \quad \forall \delta \in (0,1).
nodes.label: eq:mahalanobis_bound

nodes.name: $l_2$ bound depends on the spectrum of $A^{\top}A$
nodes.statement: The bound on the convergence rate of the $\mathcal{D}_{l_2}$ error depends on spectral properties of the matrix $A^{\top} A$. This is related to the database coherence, or similarity between the sequences $S_i$, encoded as similarity between the rows of $A$. In particular, when the problem is non-identifiable, the matrix $A^{\top} A$ has a zero eigenvalue and the reconstruction error may be arbitrarily large.
nodes.statement_short: The $l_2$ rate depends on $\lambda_{\min}(A^\top A)$, i.e. database coherence; for non-identifiable problems it is vacuous.

nodes.name: Mahalanobis bound is dimension-free
nodes.statement: In contrast, the Mahalanobis bound does not depend on the matrix $A$ or even the dimension $N$. Even if the problem is non-identifiable, we still achieve convergence under the Mahalanobis distance - yet the entries in the solution vector will not converge to the corresponding entries in the true frequencies vector ${\mathbf x}$, i.e. the reconstruction may assign (part of) the abundance of a specific species to different, yet highly similar species.
nodes.statement_short: The Mahalanobis bound is free of $A$ and $N$, so it converges even without identifiability, mixing abundance among similar species.

nodes.name: Divide-and-Conquer Reconstruction Algorithm (COMPASS)
nodes.statement: {\bf Box 1: Divide-and-Conquer Reconstruction Algorithm} \\ \indent {\bf Input: $S$ - Set of Sequences, ${\mathbf y}$ - read measurements, Probabilistic model} \\ \indent {\bf Output: ${\mathbf x}$ - vector of species frequencies} \\ \indent {\bf Parameters: $B$ - block size. $\tau_B$ - frequency threshold for each block. $k_{B,j}$ - number of partitions into blocks in $j$-th iteration, $k_F$ - final number of species allowed} \\ \begin{enumerate} \item Partition to blocks: Set ${\mathbf v}$ as a binary vector with one entry per species. If this is the first partitioning, set iteration number $j=1$. Repeat $k_{B,j}$ times: \begin{enumerate} \item Partition species randomly into non-overlapping blocks of size $B$. \item In each block (B) compute the matrix $A^{(B)}$, (where $^{(B)}$ denotes the restriction of a vector or a matrix to a block $B$), and solve (exactly) the convex optimization problem (using CVX), \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf x}^{(B)}} ||A^{(B)} {\mathbf x}^{(B)} - {\mathbf y}||_2 \: \: s.t., x^{(B)}_i \geq 0 \end{equation} \item Collect all species with frequency above the threshold: if $x^{(B)}_i \geq \tau_B$, set $v_i = 1$. Set $j=j+1$. \item Collect all linearly dependent species: For each $i$ which is non-identifiable in the block (i.e. species $i$ is orthogonal to the null space of $A^{(B)}$) set $v_i = 1$. \end{enumerate} \item Collect results from blocks: Keep only indices $i$ with $v_i=1$, i.e. species with high enough frequency in at least one block reconstruction. \item Reduce problem size: Keep only species $i$ with $v_i=1$. Set $V = \{i, v_i=1\}$ and set $A = A^{(V)}$, ${\mathbf x} = {\mathbf x}^{(V)}$. If $|V| > k_F$, go back to step 1. \item Solve for the last time the $l_2$ minimization problem for the reduced matrix, \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf x}^{(V)}} ||A^{(V)} {\mathbf x}^{(V)} - {\mathbf y}||_2 \: \: s.t., x^{(V)}_i \geq 0 \end{equation} Normalize ${\mathbf x}^{(V)}$ to sum to one, and output the normalized vector as the solution \end{enumerate}
also_stated_at: In a nutshell, the algorithm divides the species into distinct blocks, solves a reduced-size problem within each block, setting species with low frequency in the solution for each block to zero, merges solutions from different blocks and iterates to reduce problem size.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly solve nonnegative least squares on random species blocks, keep species above a threshold, shrink, and finally solve once on the survivors. Sparsity comes from the per-block thresholding.

nodes.name: Partition to blocks (repeat $k_{B,j}$ times)
nodes.statement: Partition to blocks: Set ${\mathbf v}$ as a binary vector with one entry per species. If this is the first partitioning, set iteration number $j=1$. Repeat $k_{B,j}$ times: \begin{enumerate} \item Partition species randomly into non-overlapping blocks of size $B$. \item In each block (B) compute the matrix $A^{(B)}$, (where $^{(B)}$ denotes the restriction of a vector or a matrix to a block $B$), and solve (exactly) the convex optimization problem (using CVX), \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf x}^{(B)}} ||A^{(B)} {\mathbf x}^{(B)} - {\mathbf y}||_2 \: \: s.t., x^{(B)}_i \geq 0 \end{equation} \item Collect all species with frequency above the threshold: if $x^{(B)}_i \geq \tau_B$, set $v_i = 1$. Set $j=j+1$. \item Collect all linearly dependent species: For each $i$ which is non-identifiable in the block (i.e. species $i$ is orthogonal to the null space of $A^{(B)}$) set $v_i = 1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the indicator ${\mathbf v}$ and repeat block partition-and-solve $k_{B,j}$ times.

nodes.name: Random partition into blocks of size $B$
nodes.statement: Partition species randomly into non-overlapping blocks of size $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Split species randomly into blocks of size $B$.

nodes.name: Solve the block NNLS problem with CVX
nodes.statement: In each block (B) compute the matrix $A^{(B)}$, (where $^{(B)}$ denotes the restriction of a vector or a matrix to a block $B$), and solve (exactly) the convex optimization problem (using CVX), \begin{equation} \min_{{\mathbf x}^{(B)}} ||A^{(B)} {\mathbf x}^{(B)} - {\mathbf y}||_2 \: \: s.t., x^{(B)}_i \geq 0 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Per block, build $A^{(B)}$ and solve nonnegative least squares exactly.

nodes.name: Keep species above threshold $\tau_B$
nodes.statement: Collect all species with frequency above the threshold: if $x^{(B)}_i \geq \tau_B$, set $v_i = 1$. Set $j=j+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Mark species whose block frequency is at least $\tau_B$.

nodes.name: Keep non-identifiable (linearly dependent) species
nodes.statement: Collect all linearly dependent species: For each $i$ which is non-identifiable in the block (i.e. species $i$ is orthogonal to the null space of $A^{(B)}$) set $v_i = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Also mark species that are not identifiable within the block.

nodes.name: Collect results from blocks

nodes.name: Proof of the rank criterion for identifiability
nodes.statement: From eq. (\ref{eq:mixture_model}), we have $P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf e}^{(i)} ; A, L) = [A {\mathbf x}]_i, \: \forall i=1,..,4^L$. Therefore identifiability holds if and only if $A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. The vector $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}$ is of size $4^L+1$, obtained as a concatenation of $A {\mathbf x}$ with one additional entry, $[A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}]_{4^L+1} = \sum_{j=1}^N x_j$. For any ${\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$ the last entry $[A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}]_{4^L+1}$ is equal to $1$. Therefore $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \iff A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)}, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. If $rank(A_{(1)}) = N$, we have $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore in particular the relation is true for any ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ and identifiability holds. Conversely, if $rank(A_{(1)}) < N$ then there exists a non-zero vector ${\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N, {\mathbf x} \neq {\textbf 0_N}$ in the null-space of $A_{(1)}$. Thus $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0$ and in particular $[A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}]_{4^L+1} = \sum_{j=1}^N x_j = 0$. Take a vector ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \in int(\Delta_N)$. Then there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} \equiv {\mathbf x}^{(1)} + \epsilon {\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$. But $A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)}$ and ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \neq {\mathbf x}^{(2)}$, therefore the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,S,A)$ is not identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: Identifiability is injectivity of $A$ on $\Delta_N$, equivalently of $A_{(1)}$; full rank gives it, and a null vector perturbs an interior point.

nodes.name: Reduce identifiability to injectivity of $A$ on $\Delta_N$
nodes.statement: From eq. (\ref{eq:mixture_model}), we have $P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf e}^{(i)} ; A, L) = [A {\mathbf x}]_i, \: \forall i=1,..,4^L$. Therefore identifiability holds if and only if $A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$.
nodes.statement_short: Identifiability means $A{\mathbf x}$ determines ${\mathbf x}$ on the simplex.

nodes.name: Appending the ones row changes nothing on the simplex
nodes.statement: The vector $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}$ is of size $4^L+1$, obtained as a concatenation of $A {\mathbf x}$ with one additional entry, $[A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}]_{4^L+1} = \sum_{j=1}^N x_j$. For any ${\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$ the last entry $[A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}]_{4^L+1}$ is equal to $1$. Therefore $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \iff A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)}, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\Delta_N$ the extra entry of $A_{(1)}{\mathbf x}$ is 1, so $A_{(1)}$ and $A$ are injective together.

nodes.name: Full rank implies identifiability
nodes.statement: If $rank(A_{(1)}) = N$, we have $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Therefore in particular the relation is true for any ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ and identifiability holds.
nodes.statement_short: If rank is $N$, $A_{(1)}$ is injective on all of $\mathbb{R}^N$.

nodes.name: Rank deficiency gives a non-identifying perturbation
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $rank(A_{(1)}) < N$ then there exists a non-zero vector ${\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N, {\mathbf x} \neq {\textbf 0_N}$ in the null-space of $A_{(1)}$. Thus $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0$ and in particular $[A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}]_{4^L+1} = \sum_{j=1}^N x_j = 0$. Take a vector ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \in int(\Delta_N)$. Then there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} \equiv {\mathbf x}^{(1)} + \epsilon {\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$. But $A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)}$ and ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \neq {\mathbf x}^{(2)}$, therefore the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,S,A)$ is not identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: A null vector of $A_{(1)}$ sums to zero; adding a small multiple to an interior point gives the same read distribution.

nodes.name: Proof of the critical read length
nodes.statement:
Take $L=1$. Then the vector ${\mathbf y}$ simply measures the fraction of `A's, `C's, `G's and `T's in the sample, and is of length $4$. The matrix $A^{(u,1)}$ is of size $4 	imes N$, and $rank(A^{(u,1)}) \leq 4$. Therefore, there exists a non-zero vector ${\mathbf x}$ in the null-space of $A^{(u,L)}$, $A^{(u,L)} {\mathbf x} = {\mathbf 0}$. Let ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \in int(\Delta_N)$. Then there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} \equiv {\mathbf x}^{(1)} + {\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$. But $P_x({\mathbf x}^{(1)}) = P_x({\mathbf x}^{(2)})$ for ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. Hence the problem ${	extbf {MCR} }(1,A^{(u,1)})$ is not identifiable. Take $L = n_{MAX} (=\max_i n_i)$. For each species $j$ define the read $r^{(j)} \equiv [S_j : {'A'}^{(L-n_j)}]$ where ${'A'}^{(k)}$ is a string of $k$ consecutive $'A'$s, and $[a:b]$ denotes the concatenation of the two strings $a$ and $b$. The read $r^{(j)}$ contains the sequence $S_j$, followed by a string of `A's. Since $S_{j'}$ is not a subsequence of $S_j$ for any $j 
eq j'$, the read $r^{(j)}$ cannot appear when sequencing any other sequence $j' 
eq j$, so $A_{lex(r^{(j)}) j'} = 0 \:  orall j' 
eq j$, and the $lex(r^{(j)})$-th row of $A$ is all zeros except for the j-th term. This means that $A$ has $N$ independent rows, indexed by $lex(r^{(1)}), .., lex(r^{(N)})$ and $rank(A) = N$. Therefore $rank(A_{(1)})=N$ and the problem ${	extbf {MCR} }(n_{MAX},A^{(u,n_{MAX})})$ is identifiable. Suppose that the problem is ${	extbf {MCR} }(L,A^{(u,L)})$ is identifiable, and let $L' > L$. By definition, for every ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} 
eq {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$, there exists ${\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^L}$ such that $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(1)}}({\mathbf y}; A; L) 
eq P_{{\mathbf x}^{(2)}}({\mathbf y}; A; L)$. But the distribution $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot ; A; L)$ is obtained by a projection of the distribution $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot; A; L')$ (for $i=1,2$), with $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot ; A; L) = \sum_{y', y = y'_{1:L}} P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot; A; L')$. Therefore, there must exist ${\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^{L'}}$ with $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(1)}}({\mathbf y}'; A; L') 
eq P_{{\mathbf x}^{(2)}}({\mathbf y}'; A; L')$ and the problem ${	extbf {MCR} }(L',A^{(u,L')})$ is also identifiable for $L'$.
nodes.statement_short: Three steps: $L=1$ is not identifiable by a rank count, $L=n_{MAX}$ is by padded full-sequence reads, and identifiability is monotone in $L$ by marginalization.

nodes.name: $L=1$ is not identifiable
nodes.statement: Take $L=1$. Then the vector ${\mathbf y}$ simply measures the fraction of `A's, `C's, `G's and `T's in the sample, and is of length $4$. The matrix $A^{(u,1)}$ is of size $4 \times N$, and $rank(A^{(u,1)}) \leq 4$. Therefore, there exists a non-zero vector ${\mathbf x}$ in the null-space of $A^{(u,L)}$, $A^{(u,L)} {\mathbf x} = {\mathbf 0}$. Let ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \in int(\Delta_N)$. Then there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} \equiv {\mathbf x}^{(1)} + {\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N$. But $P_x({\mathbf x}^{(1)}) = P_x({\mathbf x}^{(2)})$ for ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. Hence the problem ${\textbf {MCR} }(1,A^{(u,1)})$ is not identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: With $L=1$, $A$ has rank at most 4 < N, so a null vector gives two mixtures with the same read distribution.

nodes.name: $L=n_{MAX}$ is identifiable via padded full-sequence reads
nodes.statement:
Take $L = n_{MAX} (=\max_i n_i)$. For each species $j$ define the read $r^{(j)} \equiv [S_j : {'A'}^{(L-n_j)}]$ where ${'A'}^{(k)}$ is a string of $k$ consecutive $'A'$s, and $[a:b]$ denotes the concatenation of the two strings $a$ and $b$. The read $r^{(j)}$ contains the sequence $S_j$, followed by a string of `A's. Since $S_{j'}$ is not a subsequence of $S_j$ for any $j 
eq j'$, the read $r^{(j)}$ cannot appear when sequencing any other sequence $j' 
eq j$, so $A_{lex(r^{(j)}) j'} = 0 \:  orall j' 
eq j$, and the $lex(r^{(j)})$-th row of $A$ is all zeros except for the j-th term. This means that $A$ has $N$ independent rows, indexed by $lex(r^{(1)}), .., lex(r^{(N)})$ and $rank(A) = N$. Therefore $rank(A_{(1)})=N$ and the problem ${	extbf {MCR} }(n_{MAX},A^{(u,n_{MAX})})$ is identifiable.
nodes.statement_short: The read $S_j$ padded with A's occurs only in species $j$, giving $N$ independent rows and full rank.

nodes.name: Identifiability is monotone in $L$
nodes.statement:
Suppose that the problem is ${	extbf {MCR} }(L,A^{(u,L)})$ is identifiable, and let $L' > L$. By definition, for every ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} 
eq {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$, there exists ${\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^L}$ such that $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(1)}}({\mathbf y}; A; L) 
eq P_{{\mathbf x}^{(2)}}({\mathbf y}; A; L)$. But the distribution $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot ; A; L)$ is obtained by a projection of the distribution $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot; A; L')$ (for $i=1,2$), with $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot ; A; L) = \sum_{y', y = y'_{1:L}} P_{{\mathbf x}^{(i)}}(\cdot; A; L')$. Therefore, there must exist ${\mathbf y} \in \Delta_{4^{L'}}$ with $P_{{\mathbf x}^{(1)}}({\mathbf y}'; A; L') 
eq P_{{\mathbf x}^{(2)}}({\mathbf y}'; A; L')$ and the problem ${	extbf {MCR} }(L',A^{(u,L')})$ is also identifiable for $L'$.
nodes.statement_short: The length-$L$ read distribution is a marginal of the length-$L'$ one, so identifiability persists for $L'>L$.

nodes.name: Proof of the null-space criterion for partial identifiability
nodes.statement: In similar to Proposition \ref{prop:identifiability}, since $P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf e}^{(i)} ; A, L) = [A {\mathbf x}]_i, \: \forall i=1,..,4^L$ we have partial identifiability if and only if $A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)}_j = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}_j, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$, which holds if and only if $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)}_j = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}_j, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. Assume that $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow x_j=0 \: \forall {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Then, for any two vectors ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$ take ${\mathbf x} = {\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}$ to get, \begin{equation} A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow A_{(1)}({\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}) = 0 \Rightarrow [{\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}]_j=0 \Rightarrow x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j. \end{equation} Therefore, ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$. For the other direction, assume that ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$. Let ${\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Take some ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \in int(\Delta_N)$ and set ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} = {\mathbf x}^{(1)} + \alpha {\mathbf x}$ with $\alpha>0$ small enough such that ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. Then, \begin{equation} A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} = 0 \Rightarrow x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j \Rightarrow x_j=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: As for Proposition 1, reduce to $A_{(1)}$; the difference of two mixtures is a null vector, and an interior perturbation gives the converse.

nodes.name: Reduce partial identifiability to $A_{(1)}$
nodes.statement: In similar to Proposition \ref{prop:identifiability}, since $P_{{\mathbf x}}({\mathbf e}^{(i)} ; A, L) = [A {\mathbf x}]_i, \: \forall i=1,..,4^L$ we have partial identifiability if and only if $A {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)}_j = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}_j, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$, which holds if and only if $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow {\mathbf x}^{(1)}_j = {\mathbf x}^{(2)}_j, \: \forall {\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$.
nodes.statement_short: Partial identifiability means equal $A_{(1)}{\mathbf x}$ forces equal $j$-th coordinates on $\Delta_N$.

nodes.name: Null-space condition implies partial identifiability
nodes.statement: Assume that $A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow x_j=0 \: \forall {\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Then, for any two vectors ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}, {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$ take ${\mathbf x} = {\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}$ to get, \begin{equation} A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow A_{(1)}({\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}) = 0 \Rightarrow [{\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}]_j=0 \Rightarrow x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j. \end{equation} Therefore, ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the null-space condition to ${\mathbf x}^{(1)}-{\mathbf x}^{(2)}$.

nodes.name: Partial identifiability implies the null-space condition
nodes.statement: For the other direction, assume that ${\textbf {MCR} }(L,A)$ is partially identifiable for species $j$. Let ${\mathbf x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$. Take some ${\mathbf x}^{(1)} \in int(\Delta_N)$ and set ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} = {\mathbf x}^{(1)} + \alpha {\mathbf x}$ with $\alpha>0$ small enough such that ${\mathbf x}^{(2)} \in \Delta_N$. Then, \begin{equation} A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} = 0 \Rightarrow x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j \Rightarrow x_j=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Perturb an interior point along a null vector; equal read distributions force $x_j=0$.

nodes.name: Null-space condition forces equal $j$-th coordinates
nodes.statement: A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} \Rightarrow A_{(1)}({\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}) = 0 \Rightarrow [{\mathbf x}^{(1)} - {\mathbf x}^{(2)}]_j=0 \Rightarrow x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j.

nodes.name: Converse implication for partial identifiability
nodes.statement: A_{(1)} {\mathbf x} = 0 \Rightarrow A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(1)} = A_{(1)} {\mathbf x}^{(2)} = 0 \Rightarrow x^{(1)}_j = x^{(2)}_j \Rightarrow x_j=0.

nodes.name: Most Greengenes species are partially identifiable, but not all even at $L=100$
nodes.statement: Even for very short \ensuremath{L}, we can identify most species, since the short reads aggregate information from the entire 16S rRNA gene. However, even when \ensuremath{L}\: is long ($\ensuremath{L}=100$), there is still a small subset of species which are not identifiable.

nodes.name: Proof of the reconstruction error bounds
nodes.statement:
Eq. (ef{eq:optproblem}) with a $l_2$ loss implies that $A{\mathbf x}$ is the Euclidean projection of ${\mathbf y}$ on the convex set $A(\Delta_N) \equiv \{{\mathbf z}: \exists {\mathbf x} \in \Delta_N, \: {\mathbf z}=A{\mathbf x} \}$ (namely, it is the closest point to ${\mathbf y}$ in $A(\Delta_N)$). Similarly, $A{\mathbf x}^{*}$ is the Euclidean projection of ${\mathbf y}^{*}$ on $A(\Delta_N)$. Since projections on convex sets can only reduce distances \cite{rockafellar1970convex}, we have,  egin{equation} 
orm{A{\mathbf x}-A{\mathbf x}^{*}}_2 = 
orm{A{\mathbf x}-{\mathbf y}^{*}}_2 \leq 
orm{{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^{*}}_2. \end{equation} The left hand side above is equal to the Mahalanobis distance, since  egin{equation} \mathcal{D}_{MA}({\mathbf x}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{	op} A) = \sqrt{({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*})^{	op}(A^{	op}A)({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*})} = 
orm{A{\mathbf x}-A{\mathbf x}^{*}}_2. \end{equation} Therefore we get  egin{equation} \mathcal{D}_{MA}({\mathbf x}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{	op} A) \leq 
orm{{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^{*}}_2. \end{equation} Recall that ${\mathbf y} =  rac{1}{R} \sum_{i=1}^R {\mathbf y}^{(i)}$ where the ${\mathbf y}^{(i)}$ are i.i.d. vectors with $E[{\mathbf y}^{(i)}] = {\mathbf y}^*$. Using large-deviation bounds on vectors \cite{shawe2004kernel} we get,  egin{equation} Pr \Big( 
orm{{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^{*}}_2 \leq  rac{2}{\sqrt{R}} + \sqrt{ rac{\log(1/\delta)}{R}} \Big) \geq 1-\delta , \quad  orall 0 < \delta < 1 \end{equation} Combining eqs. (ef{eq:metric_inequality},ef{eq:metric_large_deviation}), we get part $2$ of the proposition. To prove part $1$, we need to convert this result to a bound on the Euclidian distance between ${\mathbf x}$ and ${\mathbf x}^*$. The conversion is performed by first writing an eigen-decomposition of $A^{	op} A$, $A^{	op} A = U \Lambda U^	op$ where $U$ is an orthogonal matrix and $\Lambda$ a diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues of $A^{	op} A$. This gives,  egin{align} \mathcal{D}_{MA}({\mathbf x}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{	op} A)^2 &= ({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*})^{	op}(U \Lambda U^{	op})({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*}) 
onumber \ &\geq || U^{	op} ({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*}) ||_2^2 \lambda_{\min}(A^{	op}A) 
onumber \ &= ||({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*}) ||_2^2 \lambda_{\min}(A^{	op}A) 
onumber \ &= \mathcal{D}_{l_2}({\mathbf x}, {{\mathbf x}}^*)^2 \lambda_{\min}(A^{	op}A) \end{align} Dividing both sides by $\lambda_{\min}(A^{	op}A)$, taking the square root and substituting in eq. (ef{eq:mahalanobis_bound}) gives immediately part $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Projection onto the convex set $A(\Delta_N)$ is non-expansive, so Mahalanobis error is at most $\|{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^*\|$; a vector concentration bound finishes. The $l_2$ bound follows via $\lambda_{\min}(A^\top A)$.

nodes.name: Non-expansiveness of convex projection
nodes.statement_short: $A\hat{{\mathbf x}}$ and $A{\mathbf x}^*$ are projections onto $A(\Delta_N)$, so their distance is at most $\|{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^*\|_2$.

nodes.name: Left side is the Mahalanobis distance
nodes.statement: The left hand side above is equal to the Mahalanobis distance, since \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_{MA}({\mathbf x}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{\top} A) = \sqrt{({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*})^{\top}(A^{\top}A)({\mathbf x}-{\mathbf x}^{*})} = \norm{A{\mathbf x}-A{\mathbf x}^{*}}_2. \end{equation} Therefore we get \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_{MA}({\mathbf x}, {{\mathbf x}}^*; A^{\top} A) \leq \norm{{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^{*}}_2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\|A{\mathbf x}-A{\mathbf x}^*\|_2$ with $\mathcal{D}_{MA}$ for $D=A^\top A$.

Using large-deviation bounds on vectors \cite{shawe2004kernel} we get, \begin{equation} Pr \Big( \norm{{\mathbf y}-{\mathbf y}^{*}}_2 \leq \frac{2}{\sqrt{R}} + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{R}} \Big) \geq 1-\delta , \quad \forall 0 < \delta < 1 \end{equation}

nodes.name: Combine to get part 2
nodes.statement: Combining eqs. (\ref{eq:metric_inequality},\ref{eq:metric_large_deviation}), we get part $2$ of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the two inequalities for the Mahalanobis bound.

nodes.name: Accurate reconstruction in simulation, well below the bounds
nodes.statement: Very low error ($\sim\!2\%$) is achieved for $R > 500,000$, showing that accurate reconstruction is possible for a feasible number of reads. The error rate achieved in practice is much lower than the theoretical bounds, indicating that tighter bounds might be achieved.
conclusions: The error rate achieved in practice is much lower than the theoretical bounds

nodes.name: Improved sparsity-aware reconstruction bounds
nodes.statement: Proving improved bounds on reconstruction performance which consider all these issues including the sparsity of the solution is interesting yet challenging. Standard techniques (e.g. from compressed sensing) would need to be modified to achieve improved bounds since they assume incoherence of the matrix $A$ which does not hold in our case, and do not consider the poisson sampling model we use for the reads.
nodes.statement_short: Prove reconstruction bounds that exploit sparsity, for the coherent matrices $A$ of this problem.
